## Inference and model comparison {#sec-inference-model-comparison}

This section contains an outline the basic aspects of Bayesian parameter estimation,
the backbone of all gravitational wave data analysis.
This theory is of general validity, and it does not require us to 
restrict ourselves to the gravitational wave application quite yet.

When performing the analysis of some data $d$ according to some model $M$ parameterized by some finite number of parameters $\theta$, we employ Bayes' theorem, which is derived by expressing the joint probability $\text{prob}(d, \theta | M)$ in two different ways: 

$$ \text{prob}(d, \theta | M) = \mathcal{L}(d | \theta, M) \pi (\theta | M) = p(\theta | d, M) \mathcal{Z}(d | M)\,.
$${#eq-bayes-theorem} 

The entries in this equation are: 

- the _likelihood_ $\mathcal{L}$ of the data given the model and a specific choice of its parameters - it is a probability distribution over the data (i.e. $\int \mathcal{L}(d|\theta, M) \text{d}d = 1$), but we interpret it as a function of the parameters $\theta$ while the data are fixed;
- the _prior_ $\pi$ - a representation of our beliefs about the model's parameters before seeing the data, it is a probability distribution over the parameters;
- the _posterior_ $p$ for the model's parameters - a representation of our updated beliefs about them after seeing the data, it is a probability distribution over the parameters;
- the _evidence_ $\mathcal{Z}$ for the model - a normalization constant for the posterior, or the likelihood for the data marginalized over all the model's parameters.

The likelihood and prior are part of the problem definition, and can often be readily computed at any given value of the parameters.^[This is not true for all approaches: in Simulation-Based Inference (SBI, see @sec-simulation-based-inference) the likelihood may be implicitly defined; nevertheless, Bayes' theorem underlies those analyses as well.]
What we refer to as "computing the posterior" means obtaining a useful representation for it: the questions we are often interested in are in the form

- what is the mean value and standard deviation of the $i$-th parameter $\theta_{i}$?
- what is the smallest region to which we can constrain the parameter $\theta_{i}$ with a certain probability, such as 90%?
- what is the correlation between parameter $\theta_{i}$ and parameter $\theta_{j}$?

If the parameter space is high-dimensional, evaluating the posterior on a grid quickly becomes unpractical. 
A common solution to this issue is to use stochastic methods, which allow us to obtain a set of samples $\theta _i$ distributed according to the posterior.

There exist many different such algorithms. Several of them can probe the posterior distribution $p(\theta|d, M) \propto \mathcal{L}(d|\theta, M) \pi(\theta|M)$ without computing its normalization constant $\mathcal{Z}$, the evidence: for example, the Metropolis-Hastings algorithm, a flavor of Markov-Chain Monte Carlo [@hoggDataAnalysisRecipes2018], operates by accepting or rejecting proposals based on the ratio of their probabilities, which is normalization-independent.

Nested Sampling, which we shall discuss in more detail in section @sec-nested-sampling, was developed as a method for computing the evidence, but it also yields the posterior as a by-product.

### Posterior samples

Representing a high-dimensional posterior distribution through samples is convenient, since we can easily compute summary statistics from them, such as the expectation value of any function $f(\theta)$:

$$ \langle f \rangle_{\theta \sim p(\theta | d, M)} \approx \frac{1}{N} \sum _{i=1}^N f(\theta _i) \,.
$$

### Conditioning versus marginalizing

TODO rewrite to fit the context, add definitions of marginals.

It is important to include all parameters when performing a Fisher matrix analysis.
This is because not including a parameter which correlates to the one we care about in 
the Fisher analysis is equivalent to __conditioning__ upon it having that specific value, 
while the correct operation to be performed is __marginalizing__ over all possible values.

Here is a graphical way to see the difference between conditioning and marginalizing 
for correlated variables.

```{python}
from thesis_scripts.multivariate_normal import MultivariateNormal
n = MultivariateNormal([0, 0], [[1, 0.8], [0.8, 1]])
n.plot_2d_analytical(0, 0, .9)
```

When dealing with the _correlation matrix_ marginalizing 
simply amounts to ignoring some parameters, but crucially
in the _Fisher matrix_ this is not the case, since the 
inversion introduces mixing between the parameters.

#### Weighted samples {#sec-weighted-samples}

Some algorithms, such as Nested Sampling [@sec-nested-sampling] or importance-sampled Neural Posterior Estimation [@sec-importance-sampling-npe], can return a set of _weighted_ samples. 
This means that each sample $\theta_{i}$ is associated with a weight $w_{i}$.
Weighted samples can also arise in the context of _reweighting_: slightly perturbing the assumptions underlying an analysis and 

Summary statistics can be computed through __importance sampling__, as 
$$ \langle f \rangle_{\theta \sim p(\theta | d, M)} \approx \frac{1}{N} \sum _{i=1}^N w_{i} f(\theta _i) \,.
$$
Weighted samples can also be directly used to construct histograms --- the height of each bin will correspond to the sum of the weights of the samples contained within it ---, perform kernel density estimates and so forth. 
They can be inconvenient

We can also extract equally-weighted samples from weighted ones by __rejection sampling__ @ashtonReconstructingResamplingGuide2025:

1. Establish the highest weight, $w _\text{max} = \max w_{i}$;
2. for each sample $\theta_{i}$: 
	1. compute $x= w_{i} / w _\text{max} \in [0, 1)$;
	2. extract a uniformly random number $r \in [0, 1)$;
	3. if $r<x$, keep the sample $\theta_{i}$, otherwise, remove it.

On average, this procedure will retain $n\langle w \rangle / \max w$ out of $n$ samples; if many of the weights are lower than their maximum, it can become quite inefficient. 
In fact, under the realistic assumption of the weights being log-normally distributed, it can be shown that working with the weighted samples can be significantly more efficient than performing rejection sampling [@ashtonReconstructingResamplingGuide2025, fig. 3].

#### $p$-$p$ plots

Mistrusting the results of our analysis pipelines is wise: we ought to put them through as many tests as possible in order to spot any issues. 


A common test for self-consistency is the $p$-$p$ plot, which specifically regards the marginal distributions, $p(\theta_i | d)$ for a fixed $i$. 
We can test this by performing a campaign of injections, for which the true value $\hat{\theta_{i}}$ is known: every time, we need to generate a realistic simulation of the data $d$ and analyze it feigning ignorance of the true value. 
Then, we may compute the percentile of the distribution at which the true value lies:
$$
u = \int_{-\infty}^{\hat{\theta}_{i}} p(\theta_{i}| d) \text{d}\theta = \text{CDF}_{p(\theta_{i}| d)}(\hat{\theta}_{i})\,.
$$
Here we assume for simplicity that the parameter can range over $\mathbb{R}$, but the same calculation can be performed starting integration from the lower bound.
This is the definition of the cumulative distribution function, computed at $\hat{\theta}_{i}$. 
Repeating this procedure $N_\text{inj}$ times, we will get a set of values $u_{j}$, where the index $j$ denotes the number of the injection.
If our analysis is self-consistent, and $p(\theta_{i}|d)$ is the probability density for the true value, then the $u_{j}$ should be uniformly distributed in the interval $[0, 1]$.

There are a few ways to check whether this is the case, both visual and statistical. 
The simplest is probably to histogram the $u_{j}$ and visually check for uniformity. This is not a very powerful method, however, since it is hard to tell by eye which level of fluctuation is "acceptable", and there is a dependence on the size of the bins used for the histogram.
A better choice is to compute the empirical cumulative distribution function: 
$$
P(u) = \frac{\text{number of }u_{j} \leq u}{N_\text{inj}}
$$

This is a "stepwise", locally constant function. For a perfectly uniform distribution, and an asymptotically high number of injections, it asymptotically tends toward $P(u) = u$. 
It is uniquely defined, with no parameters.

A first visual test is to plot it and check that it approximately follows the diagonal.
A useful variant of this is to plot $u$ on the horizontal axis and $P(u) - u$ on the vertical, which is expected to be near zero; see e.g. @chatziioannouNoiseSpectralEstimation2019.
This allows for the resolution of small fluctuations from the diagonal. 

In order to help in the visual check, we need something to compare against: what is the magnitude of the expected fluctuations of $P(u)$ under the null hypothesis, i.e. if the distribution is indeed uniform?
If we fix a value of $u$, the question can be reframed as follows: out of $N_\text{inj}$ independent and identically distributed uniform random variates, how many are smaller than $u$?
The probability for each of them being smaller than $u$ is $u$ itself, so the probability mass function describing this scenario will be binomial, but scaled by $N_\text{inj}$:
$$
p \left( P (u) = \frac{k}{N_\text{inj}} \right) = {k\choose N_\text{inj}} u^{k} (1-u)^{N _\text{inj}-k}
$$
Therefore we can easily compute its mean and variance, $\langle P(u) \rangle =u$ and
$$
\langle (P(u) -u)^{2} \rangle = \frac{u(1-u)}{N_\text{inj}}\,.
$$


```{python}
#| label: fig-pp-plot-theory
#| fig-cap: "Visualizations for a p-p test: histogram, empirical cdf, tilted empirical cdf. We also visualize the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test."

from thesis_scripts import pp_plot
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

rng = np.random.default_rng(seed=1)
u = rng.uniform(size=1000)

fig, ax = pp_plot.pp_plot(u, confidence_intervals=(.68, .95, .997))
plt.show()
```

Along with the plots we show the values, and corresponding $p$-values, for the one-sided Kolmogorov-Smirnov [@kolmogorovSullaDeterminazioneEmpirica1933;@smirnovTableEstimatingGoodness1948] statistics $D_{+}$ and $D_-$, defined in terms of the empirical CDF as

$$
D_{\pm} = \sup \left[ \pm \left( P_{\text{emp}}(u) - u \right)  \right]\,.
$$
One may also use the two-sided statistic
$$
D = \sup \lvert  P_{\text{emp}}(u) - u  \rvert\,.
$$

We show the two one-sided versions since their values can be combinedly used to distinguish different types of misspecification, see @sec-pp-test-failure-modes. 
The density function of the K-S statistics under the null hypothesis is shown in @fig-kolmogorov-smirnov-distribution.

```{python}
#| label: fig-kolmogorov-smirnov-distribution
#| fig-cap: "Distribution for the K-S statistics."

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy import stats

D = np.linspace(0, 0.07, num=500)
n = 1000
plt.plot(D, stats.ksone.pdf(D, n=n), label=f'$D_{{\pm}}$ distribution for $n={{{n}}}$')
plt.plot(D, stats.kstwo.pdf(D, n=n), label=f'$D$ distribution for $n={{{n}}}$')

plt.legend()
plt.xlabel('$D$ or $D_{\pm}$')
plt.ylabel('Probability density')
plt.show()
```

These tests are common in the literature: they were performed, for example, with the software `BILBY` @romero-shawBayesianInferenceCompact2020; more details can also be found in @romero-shawWhenModelsFail2022.

#### Failure modes {#sec-pp-test-failure-modes}

Let us now explore the way that $p$-$p$ plots look when the test fails. 

For simplicity, we will always consider measurements
for which the posterior distribution is Gaussian.

However, while we will keep the distribution according to which the true parameter $\hat{\theta}$ is distributed fixed to the standard normal, centered on zero and with unit variance, we will explore how the $p$-$p$ plot can help us diagnose errors in the estimated posterior distribution.

First, let us suppose we have a bias in our measurement, so that the posterior distribution is not centered at the true value, 0, but instead at a slightly higher one, say 0.2:
$$
\begin{aligned}
p(\theta|d) &= \mathcal{N}(\mu=0.2, \sigma=1)\\
p(\hat{\theta}|d) &= \mathcal{N}(\mu=0, \sigma=1)\,.
\end{aligned}
$$

```{python}
#| label: fig-pp-plot-bias-positive
#| fig-cap: "p-p plot in the scenario of an overestimation bias."

from thesis_scripts import pp_plot
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy import stats

rng = np.random.default_rng(seed=1)
u = stats.norm(loc=0.2, scale=1).cdf(rng.normal(size=2000))

fig, ax = pp_plot.pp_plot(u, confidence_intervals=(.68, .95, .997))
plt.show()
```

Suppose instead that the bias is in the negative direction:
$$
\begin{aligned}
p(\theta|d) &= \mathcal{N}(\mu=-0.2, \sigma=1)\\
p(\hat{\theta}|d) &= \mathcal{N}(\mu=0, \sigma=1)\,.
\end{aligned}
$$

```{python}
#| label: fig-pp-plot-bias-negative
#| fig-cap: "p-p plot in the scenario of a bias."

from thesis_scripts import pp_plot
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy import stats

rng = np.random.default_rng(seed=1)
u = stats.norm(loc=-0.2, scale=1).cdf(rng.normal(size=2000))

fig, ax = pp_plot.pp_plot(u, confidence_intervals=(.68, .95, .997))
plt.show()
```

Note that only one of the two KS tests gives extreme results in both cases. 

Now let us consider a different scenario: when the mean of the posterior distribution is correctly estimated, but its variance is not. 
If the variance is too high, we are _underconstraining_ the parameter, assigning a higher uncertainty to our measurement than is warranted: for example, if
$$
\begin{aligned}
p(\theta|d) &= \mathcal{N}(\mu=0, \sigma=1.2)\\
p(\hat{\theta}|d) &= \mathcal{N}(\mu=0, \sigma=1)\,.
\end{aligned}
$$

```{python}
#| label: fig-pp-plot-bias-underconstrain
#| fig-cap: "p-p plot in the scenario of an underconstraining bias."

from thesis_scripts import pp_plot
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy import stats

rng = np.random.default_rng(seed=1)

u = stats.norm(loc=0, scale=1.2).cdf(rng.normal(size=2500))

fig, ax = pp_plot.pp_plot(u, confidence_intervals=(.68, .95, .997))
plt.show()
```

In the opposite scenario, we are _overconstraining_, assigning a lower uncertainty to our measurement than is warranted: for example,
$$
\begin{aligned}
p(\theta|d) &= \mathcal{N}(\mu=0, \sigma=0.8)\\
p(\hat{\theta}|d) &= \mathcal{N}(\mu=0, \sigma=1)\,.
\end{aligned}
$$
```{python}
#| label: fig-pp-plot-bias-overconstrain
#| fig-cap: "p-p plot in the scenario of an overconstraining bias."

from thesis_scripts import pp_plot
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy import stats

rng = np.random.default_rng(seed=1)

u = stats.norm(loc=0, scale=0.8).cdf(rng.normal(size=2500))

fig, ax = pp_plot.pp_plot(u, confidence_intervals=(.68, .95, .997))
plt.show()
```

Finally, let us consider a distribution with the correct mean and variance, but the wrong shape.
To this end we choose a generalized normal distribution, with a shape parameter $\beta = 2.5$. 
The $\beta = 2$ case recovers the standard normal distribution. 

```{python}
#| label: fig-generalized-normal
#| fig-cap: "Triangle and normal distributions with the same variance and mean."

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy import stats

beta = 2.5
var = stats.gennorm.stats(beta, moments='v')

dist = stats.gennorm(beta=beta, loc=0, scale=1/np.sqrt(var))
vals = np.linspace(-4., 4., num=1000)
plt.plot(vals, stats.norm(loc=0, scale=1).pdf(vals), label='Standard normal')
plt.plot(vals, dist.pdf(vals), label=f'Generalized normal with $\\beta={beta}$')
plt.ylim(0,0.5)
plt.xlim(-4, 4)
plt.legend()
plt.show()
```

We rescale the distribution so that it has unit variance, as shown in figure @fig-generalized-normal.
As this shift is harder to detect than the ones before, we need to raise the statistics. 

```{python}
#| label: fig-pp-plot-bias-distributional
#| fig-cap: "p-p plot in the scenario of the wrong distribution, despite correct mean and variance."

from thesis_scripts import pp_plot
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy import stats

rng = np.random.default_rng(seed=1)

u = dist.cdf(rng.normal(size=10000))

fig, ax = pp_plot.pp_plot(u, confidence_intervals=(.68, .95, .997))
plt.show()
```

The distribution looks similar to the underconstrained case, as for the bulk of the probability mass (-2 to +2 in figure @fig-generalized-normal) the difference between these distribution is analogous to underconstraining. 
However, close to the edges in @fig-pp-plot-bias-distributional we can see the trend reverse. 

### Model comparison {#sec-model-comparison}

Why should we care about the evidence $\mathcal{Z}$ when performing inference?
It is helpful when comparing models. 
In a realistic scenario, our model $M$ may not adequately capture the behavior of the system at hand,
but in equation @eq-bayes-theorem, all the terms are conditional on it: 
an analysis performed under the assumption that the model is true cannot 
inform us on its validity by construction.
If more than one model is available, we can make some steps toward 
addressing this problem by comparing them; still, we should remember that 
our results are dependent on the set of models we used, and it is possible they may 
all miss some important aspect.

We can write an anologous expressio to @eq-bayes-theorem for both models $M_{1}$ and $M_{2}$:
$$
p(M_{i}|d) p(d) = p(d| M_{i}) p(M_{i});
$$
dividing one by the other, we get the following:
$$ 
\frac{p(M_{1} | d)}{p(M_{2}|d)} = \frac{p(d|M_{1})}{p(d|M_{2})} \frac{p(M_{1})}{p(M_{2})}.
$${#eq-model-comparison}

The left-hand term in @eq-model-comparison is dubbed _posterior odds_: 
it describes the degree to which we should prefer model $1$ over model $2$ after seeing the data $d$. On the right hand we have a product of two terms: the _Bayes Factor_ (BF)
$$
\text{BF}_{2}^{1} = \frac{p(d|M_{1})}{p(d|M_{2})}
$${#eq-bayes-factor}
describes the degree to which the data prefer model $1$ over model 2.
The remaining term, $p(M_{1}) / p(M_{2})$, is called _prior odds_, and it describes the degree to which we preferred model 1 over model 2 before seeing the data $d$.
This may be informed, for example, by previous observations, theoretical considerations, or simply be set to 1 if our belief is that both models are equally likely.

::: {#nte-odds-logits .callout-note collapse="true"}
##### On the usage of odds

@eq-bayes-factor can be applied several times in a row, as more observations become available; the Bayes Factors from each observation multiply. 

This has an interesting consequence if the two models at hand are complementary, i.e. one being correct excludes the other, and one or the other must be correct, so that their probabilities satisfy $p(M_{1})+p(M_{2})=1$. If this is the case, we may simplify the notation by simply using $P(M_{1})$ and $1-p(M_{1})=p(M_{2})$. 
Then, taking the logarithm of @eq-bayes-factor, we can express it as 
$$
\text{logit}(p(M_{1}|d)) = \log \text{BF}_{2}^{1} + \text{logit}(p(M_{1}))\,,
$$
where we defined the $\text{logit}$ function, also shown in figure @fig-logit-function:
$$
\text{logit}(p) = \log \frac{p}{1-p}\,.
$$

```{python}
#| label: fig-logit-function
#| fig-cap: "The logit function."

from thesis_scripts import *
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

p = np.linspace(5e-3, 1-5e-3, num=500)
plt.xlabel('$\\mathrm{{logit}}(p)$')

plt.plot(np.log(p / (1-p)), p)
plt.xlabel('$\\mathrm{{logit}}(p)$')
plt.ylabel('$p$')
plt.grid()
plt.show()
```

The logit of a probability $\text{logit}(p) \in \mathbb{R}$, also called __log-odds__, 
can be argued to be more natural way to express it than $p\in (0, 1)$. 
Probabilities very close to 0 or 1 are extreme statements: in this parameterization, they are accordingly very far from the origin, and absolutes such as $p=0, 1$ are divergent towards $\pm \infty$.
:::

Based on this formalism, we may be tempted to multiply Bayes Factors 
from different observations of the same phenomenon. 
While this is correct in an idealized scenario, 
it can lead to dramatically incorrect conclusions when applied in practice,
due to its dependence on the prior used in each analysis;
@isiComparingBayesFactors2022 have discussed this 
in the context of tests of General Relativity (GR).

If two models are nested, _i.e._ one is a special case of the other, 
then we can express the Bayes Factor between them in a simple way
[@dickeyWeightedLikelihoodRatio1971;@cameronGeneralizedSavageDickeyRatio2013]:
$$
\text{BF}_{1}^{2} = \frac{p_{2}(\theta=\theta_{0}|d)}{\pi_{2}(\theta=\theta_{0})}\,.
$${#eq-savage-dickey-density-ratio}
Here, model 1 is the special case of model 2 in which parameter $\theta$ equals $\theta_{0}$, $p_{2}$ is the marginal posterior distribution for the parameter $\theta$ under model 2, while $\pi_{2}$ is the marginal prior distribution for the parameter $\theta$ under model 2.

This formulation illustrates the general fact that Bayes Factors are heavily dependent on the width of the prior distribution.
This is a well-known feature of Bayesian inference, known as the Occam Factor or Penalty: 
the preferred models are the "simplest", in the sense that they are compatible with the data for a large fraction of their prior mass; a model which is able to fit a plethora of different scenarios is disfavored compared to one which fits the current one and few others.

A negative consequence of this arises if the prior distributions cannot be selected in a principled way, though: if they are set too wide, the data may seem to favor the baseline model even in the presence of a deviation.
